title: Chapter 10: Boss Level 2: The Number Guessing Game
video_title: Python Chapter 10: Boss Level 2, The Number Guessing Game
summary: A typed word crashes a program that trusts every answer. Follow Asha as she plans, builds and tests the Corner Cafe biscuit jar game: a random secret from 1 to 20, five tries with hints, and answers checked with strip and isdigit before int. She uses an AI assistant at all six stages and catches two confident AI mistakes with tests: randrange(1, 20) never picks 20, and removing strip rejects 7 with a space.

scenes.title: Step 3: A random secret
scenes.direction: Teach import, randint with both ends, randrange like range, and the seed. Then stage 3 plants the AI mistake, a test loop proves it, and stage 4 confirms. Quiz, breather.

visual.heading: Step 3: The random module
visual.label: Build it
items: A **module** is a file of ready-made Python code. `import random` loads one.
`random.randint(1, 20)` picks a whole number from 1 to 20. **Both ends** are included.
`random.randrange(1, 20)` works like `range()`: it **stops before** 20.
`random.seed(3)` makes the same numbers on every run: useful for tests.

segments.say: Step 3: a real secret. A fixed 7 is no game. Python has a module for random numbers. A module is a file of ready-made Python code, and import loads it.
Random dot rand int, 1 comma 20, picks a whole number from 1 to 20. Both ends are included: 1 and 20 can both be picked.
The module also has rand range. It works like range from Chapter 8: it stops before its end value. So rand range 1 comma 20 never picks 20.
And a seed makes the same random numbers on every run. That sounds strange, but it is useful for testing.

visual.heading: Step 3: Random numbers, with a seed

segments.say: Line 2 imports the module. Line 3 sets the seed to 3.
Lines 4 to 6 pick three numbers: 8, 19 and 18.
On the same Python, the same numbers come back on every run. Your numbers may differ on another version. Delete line 3, and the numbers change on every run. A real game has no seed.

visual.heading: Generate: one line with exact limits

messages.text: Write one line of Python that picks a random whole number from 1 to 20, including both. Name the variable secret. Tell me exactly which numbers it can pick.

Here is the line: `secret = random.randrange(1, 20)`
It can pick every whole number from 1 to 20.

segments.say: Stage 3: generate. Asha asks the AI for the secret line, from 1 to 20, including both. And she asks exactly which numbers it can pick.
The AI writes one line with rand range, 1 comma 20. And it says every number from 1 to 20 can be picked. It sounds sure.

ask.question: The AI says `randrange(1, 20)` can pick every number from 1 to 20. Is it right?

after.say: No. Rand range stops before its end value, like range. But Asha does not argue. She tests it.

visual.heading: Test: run the AI's line 10,000 times
visual.hidden_text: What should Highest be, if 20 can be picked?

segments.say: Line 6 is a for loop from Chapter 8. It runs line 7, the AI's line, ten thousand times.
Lines 4 and 5 start lowest at 20 and highest at 1, the opposite ends, so the first number picked replaces both.
Lines 8 to 11 keep the lowest and the highest number so far. Line 3 is a seed, so the test gives the same result every run.

ask.question: If 20 can be picked, what should line 13 print?

after.say: Highest, 20. But it prints 19! In ten thousand draws, 20 never appeared.
A customer with a jar of 20 biscuits could never win.

visual.heading: Test: show the AI the evidence

messages.text: You said randrange(1, 20) can pick 20. I ran your line 10,000 times and kept the lowest and the highest:

You are right, and I was wrong. `randrange()` stops before its end value, like `range()`, so 20 is never picked.
Use `random.randint(1, 20)`, which includes both ends.
I ran the same test with randint:

segments.say: Stage 4: test. Asha shows the AI the line and the result: highest, 19.
Now the AI agrees. Rand range stops before 20. It suggests rand int, 1 comma 20.
Asha runs the same test with rand int. Highest, 20. Both ends appear.

visual.question: Which line picks a whole number from 1 to 6, like a dice?

segments.say: Quick check. Which line picks a whole number from 1 to 6, like a dice?

after.say: B. Rand int, 1 comma 6. Both ends are included. Rand range would never roll a 6.

scenes.title: Step 4: Check before you convert
scenes.direction: Stage 5 debug: cause first. Then teach isdigit with its rule, ask which lines are True, reveal.

visual.heading: Debug: the cause before the fix

messages.text: A customer typed seven, and my game stopped. Here are my lines and the full error. Explain the cause first. Then show the smallest fix that keeps the game running.

Line 3 converts the answer with `int()` at once. `int()` cannot turn the text 'seven' into a number, so Python raises a `ValueError`.
The fix: keep the answer as text, check it first, and call `int()` only when every character is a digit.

segments.say: Stage 5: debug. Asha pastes the two lines and the full error from the start of this video. She asks for the cause first, then the smallest fix.
The AI names line 3. Int cannot convert the word seven. The fix: keep the answer as text, check it first, and only then convert it.
Step 4: the check. The string method is digit gives True only when the text has at least one character, and every character is a digit.
So no letters, no minus sign, no decimal point, and no spaces. An empty answer has no characters at all.
Line 8 removes the space with strip from Chapter 3 first, then checks.

after.say: Only two. Line 2, the text 12. And line 8, where strip removed the space first.
Line 7 is the surprise: a space before the 7 is enough to give False.

scenes.title: Step 5: Check, then convert
scenes.direction: The check ladder: is digit, then range, then int. Ask what happens with seven, reveal.

visual.heading: Step 5: Check, then convert
visual.hidden_text: Predict the message before it appears.

segments.say: Step 5 puts the check in order. Line 2 reads the answer and strips the spaces. It stays text.
Line 3: if it is not all digits, line 4 asks for a whole number.
Line 5: if it is outside 1 to 20, line 6 says so. Line 5 can safely call int, because line 3 already found that the answer is made of digits.
Only a fair answer reaches the else, where line 8 converts it.

ask.question: The customer types `seven`. Which line prints, and does `int()` ever see the word?

after.say: Line 4 prints: please type a whole number. And int never sees the word, so nothing crashes.

scenes.title: Test it

visual.heading: How do you test a random game?
visual.label: Test it
body: You cannot know the right result if the secret changes every run.
So each test is a **copy** of the game with one change: line 4 sets a **fixed secret**.
Every other line is the same, and each test has its own typed answers.

segments.say: How do you test a random game? If the secret changes every run, you cannot know the right result. So each test is a copy of the game, where line 4 sets a fixed secret, such as 7, and has its own typed answers.
Asha writes six tests, each with the result she expects.
A win on the first try.
The high, low, win game you saw at the start.
Words and an empty answer, which must not count as tries.
Five wrong guesses, to reach the end of the tries.
And the boundary values. The largest secret, 20, with the answers 0 and 21 outside the jar.
And the smallest secret, 1.

visual.heading: Test 3: words and an empty answer

segments.say: Test 3. The secret is 7. The player presses enter with no answer, then types seven, then 7.

after.say: Out of tries. It was 7. The tries left counted down to 0, and the loop stopped after the fifth guess. Pass!

segments.say: Test 5. The secret is 20. Answers 0 and 21 are outside the jar, so each gets a message.
Remember the question about 0 in step 6? Here is the proof: 0 got a message, and did not count as a try.
Then 20. Correct, with one guess used. Pass!
Test 6. The secret is 1, and the player guesses 1. Correct. Pass! All six tests match their expected results.
